html:
A church court set up in 1478 by the Catholic Monarchs, Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon, with the pope's approval, and run by the Spanish crown. It began work in Seville in 1480 and was finally abolished in 1834.

Its first target was conversos, Jews who had become Christians, many under pressure after the riots of 1391, and who were suspected of secretly keeping Jewish ways. Under its first Inquisitor General, the Dominican friar Tomás de Torquemada, thousands were tried. The expulsion of the Jews in 1492 was meant partly to cut conversos off from them. Later it turned on moriscos, converts from Islam, who were finally expelled from 1609 to 1614, and on Protestants, mystics, witches and banned books.

Its trials used secret informers and torture, and ended in public ceremonies called autos-da-fé, where sentences were read and some of the condemned burned. Historians estimate a few thousand executions over its whole life, most in the first decades. It was copied in Portugal and the colonies, as in the Mexican Inquisition.
